newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends higher before April expiry.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends higher before April expiry.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures settled higher Monday as April contracts climbed toward spot cash market levels in the West ahead of their expiration on Tuesday.
"The convergence between cash and futures is approaching," said one Oregon-based futures trader.
Western cash power prices continued to soften on plenty of hydroelectricity and soft spot demand, but they are still valued above April futures, brokers and traders said.

In the cash market, day-ahead firm, peak electricity prices at California-Oregon Border (COB) fell 25-75 cents to $11.25-12.25 a megawatt hour (MWh), while those at Palo Verde (PV) slipped 50 cents to $14.00-15.00.
April COB futures settled up 52 cents at $10.87 after posting a high of $11.00 May COB ended at $9.95, up 43 cents. Other deferred COB months finished 10 to 25 cents higher.
April PV settled up 16 cents at $14.61 after hitting a high at $14.75. May PV ended up 15 cents at $14.30. Other active PV contracts finished eight to 25 cents higher.

There were concerns over surplus hydropower staying in the Northwest because the Pacific Intertie failed to ramp up another 1,000 megawatts (MW) over the weekend, but they were overshadowed by pre-expiration maneuvering, market sources said.
"It was mostly shortcovering. We saw some good buying toward the end. You'll probably see it again tomorrow," said one New York futures broker.

The intertie transmission system running between the Northwest and southern California was capped at 5,200 MW until at least Tuesday due to problems with maintenance on a 500 kilovolt segment of the line.

The Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC) on Friday endorsed an increase in the rate to 6,250 MW, but a study group convened by the reliability council will first need to examine operating procedures for BPA, Idaho Power and Pacific Gas and Electric, a BPA transmission scheduler said.
Nevertheless, spot power supply in the Southwest began to rise this past weekend with the Sunday restart the 750 MW unit 5 at the Four Corners coal-fired power plant in Arizona.
Moreover, Edison International planned to restore the 1,070 MW San Onofre 2 nuclear unit to service Wednesday following a delay to repair a leak in a valve in an internal water cooling system.
Temperatures in the Northwest were forecast to be near normal Monday, then climb four to eight degrees Fahrenheit above normal by midweek.
Readings in the Southwest would average three to six degrees above normal Tuesday, and climb to five to 10 degrees above the seasonal norm for the rest of the week.
NYMEX estimated 398 COB and 308 PV contracts were sold, compared with Friday's 308 COB and 248 lots.
